strengths: Closes a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing HP guarantees for decentralized SGD require restrictive assumptions (uniformly bounded gradients, asymptotically vanishing noise), while the paper shows vanilla DSGD converges in HP under essentially the same conditions needed for MSE convergence, for both non-convex and strongly convex costs.

First work to establish linear speed-up in the number of users for HP convergence of decentralized methods, with order-optimal rates and transient times that match or strictly improve upon those implied by MSE results (e.g., O(max{n/(1-λ), 1/(1-λ)^2}) for strongly convex costs vs. O(n/(1-λ)^2)).

Substantive technical novelty with independent value: Lemma 2 (variance-reduction of decentralized averaging in the HP sense), Lemma 3/4 (MGF bounds on the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity), and Lemma 5 (refined MF bound for 'almost decreasing' processes that is sharper than the uniform MGF bounds of [31, 32, 40], as convincingly argued in Appendix I).

Proofs are provided in detail in the appendix; I checked several key steps (e.g., Lemma 6/2 sub-Gaussian arguments, Lemma 7/5 unrolling, Lemma 8, the proof skeletons for Theorems 1 and 2) and found them sound and internally consistent.

Honest and thorough treatment of limitations: the √d/d dimension dependence is explicitly explained (Appendix K) with a discussion of the norm-sub-Gaussian alternative and its trade-offs; the restriction to fixed step-size/known horizon for linear speed-up is analyzed rather than hidden; extension to time-varying networks is outlined (Appendix J).
Numerical experiments (Appendix G) are well-designed to directly test the two central theoretical claims — exponential tail decay and linear speed-up — and the results are consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The bounds carry an unavoidable √d (non-convex) and d (strongly convex) dimension dependence, which is worse than prior decentralized results [11, 57]; while the cause (norm vs. inner-product sub-Gaussianity) is well explained and the authors argue it is inherent to their noise condition, this still weakens the practical reach of the results in high dimensions.

Linear speed-up for non-convex costs requires a fixed step-size and a known time horizon (via C in Theorem 1); the unknown-horizon time-varying step-size variant loses linear speed-up, so a key advertised benefit is contingent on tuning to T.

The strongly convex case requires identical initialization across users and each fi strongly convex, and does not cover PL costs (left to future work), whereas [57] covers PL; the comparison with the closest prior work, while favorable in assumptions and rates, is therefore not entirely like-for-like in scope.

The transient-time improvement over MSE rates (strictly sharper for strongly convex costs) is a somewhat surprising claim derived from upper bounds alone; no lower-bound argument corroborates that the HP transient time genuinely is smaller, so 'strictly better' should be read as a property of the analysis rather than a tightness guarantee.
Experiments are limited to quadratic costs on synthetic problems; while appropriate for validating theory, they do not probe the algorithm in more realistic ML settings.

Theorems 2's statement hides higher-order terms in O(·) (the full bound is relegated to Appendix F), which slightly reduces the precision of the main-text result, though the full statement is available.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: high-probability (HP) convergence of decentralized SGD has, prior to this work, only been established under strong assumptions (uniformly bounded gradients, asymptotically vanishing noise) that are much stronger than those needed for MSE convergence; this work closes that gap.

The main theorems show DSGD achieves order-optimal rates with linear speed-up in the number of users in the HP sense for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, which appears to be the first such result for decentralized methods; the derived transient time is shown to be strictly sharper than what follows from existing MSE rates.

Several technical contributions are novel and of independent interest: Lemma 2 (variance reduction benefit of decentralization in the HP sense, showing the average noise is O(σ√(d/√n))-sub-Gaussian), Lemma 4 (MGF bound on the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity), and Lemma 5 (a sharp 'almost decreasing' process MGF bound that improves on centralized techniques from [31, 32, 40]).

The appendices contain complete, detailed proofs; the derivations I checked (e.g., Lemma 9/10, Lemma 6, the structure of Theorem 1's proof via the 'offset trick') are coherent and self-contained, including the derivation of the transient time (Appendix H) and discussion of why prior MGF techniques fail to give linear speed-up (Appendix I).
Numerical experiments on synthetic strongly convex problems validate both claimed qualitative behaviors: exponential tail decay and faster tail decay with larger networks.

Limitations are acknowledged transparently (dimension dependence, need for sub-Gaussian noise, static networks, non-convex linear speed-up only under fixed step-size/known horizon), with several extensions worked out in the appendix (time-varying networks, dimension discussion).
weaknesses: The bounds carry an unavoidable factor of √d (non-convex) and d (strongly convex) absent from the MSE bounds in [11, 57] and from centralized HP bounds; while the authors argue this stems from the chosen sub-Gaussianity definition and discuss mitigations (norm-sub-Gaussian noise) in Appendix K, it means the results are not strictly comparable to, and in some regimes weaker than, prior HP rates.

The setup requires conditional independence of samples across users and iterations (A4), which is a strong assumption in practice (e.g., correlated data across neighboring users in federated/decentralized deployments is common); the sensitivity of the variance-reduction argument to this assumption is not explored.

For non-convex costs, linear speed-up requires a fixed step-size and known time horizon; with the standard time-varying schedule (unknown horizon) speed-up is lost. This is disclosed, but it restricts the practical applicability of the headline claim.

The heterogeneity assumption (A5) is a max-over-users condition, admitted by the authors to be slightly stronger than the average heterogeneity condition in [11]; justification for this choice is given only on grounds of proof simplicity.

The theorem statements are dominated by unwieldy constants (e.g., Lemma 4's t0 ≥ max{6, 288σ²K/μ², 3456σ²λ²K/μ²(1−λ), ...} and Theorem 1's five-term minimum for C), which harms readability and makes it hard to gauge when the constants are reasonable; Theorem 2 hides higher-order terms behind O(·) with the full bound deferred to the appendix.

The experiments are limited to synthetic quadratic objectives with Gaussian noise; they validate qualitative behavior (exponential tails, speed-up) but do not test the theory on realistic ML tasks, on heterogeneous data distributions, or against baselines (e.g., clipped variants, or [57]).

Strongly convex results require each local cost to be μ-strongly convex (A6), and the framework does not handle gradient tracking, so bounded heterogeneity cannot be removed in the non-convex case; PL costs and GT are deferred to future work.

strengths: Closes a genuine gap in the literature: prior HP guarantees for decentralized SGD (e.g., [57]) required path-wise uniformly bounded gradients and asymptotically vanishing noise; this paper shows DSGD converges in the HP sense under the same cost-function assumptions used for MSE results, which is the expected (and previously open) state of affairs given the centralized SGD theory.

First work to establish linear speed-up in the number of users for decentralized methods in the HP sense, for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, with order-optimal rates; the paper carefully explains (Appendix I) why the centralized-style uniformly bounded MGF argument (eq. (53)) cannot yield linear speed-up, which substantiates that the improvement is not superficial.

Several technical contributions are of independent interest and clearly delineated: Lemma 2 (variance-reduction benefit of decentralization in the HP sense, O(σ√d/√n)-sub-Gaussian average noise), Lemma 4 (MGF bound on the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity), and Lemma 5 (sharp MF bound for 'almost decreasing' processes, sharper than centralized results in [31, 32, 40]).

Results are informative beyond the headline rates: the analysis yields HP transient times that match or strictly improve on those implied by MSE rates (Appendix H), and the roles of noise, heterogeneity, network connectivity, and step-size choice (fixed vs. time-varying) are discussed transparently, including the honest admission that linear speed-up requires a fixed step-size/known horizon.

The manuscript is unusually complete and self-contained: full proofs are provided in the appendix, assumptions are carefully compared to prior work (e.g., (A5) vs. [11]'s average heterogeneity), and limitations such as the √d/d dimension dependence are explicitly analyzed (Appendix K) with possible mitigations discussed.

Numerical experiments (Appendix G) directly validate the two central theoretical claims: exponential tail decay of the empirical tail probability and linear speed-up with the number of users, using a setup with unbounded gradients and heterogeneous data consistent with the assumptions.
weaknesses: The dimension dependence introduced by the analysis (√d for non-convex, d for strongly convex) is absent from prior HP bounds ([11, 57]) and from MSE bounds; while the authors argue it is unavoidable under their sub-Gaussian definition and discuss mitigation via norm-sub-Gaussianity (Appendix K), this remains a real regression in constant-factor terms of the bounds.

Linear speed-up requires a fixed step-size and hence knowledge of the time horizon T; with a time-varying step-size the non-convex result loses linear speed-up, and the strongly convex fixed-step-size analysis is omitted entirely (only remarked upon at the end of Appendix F).

The results apply only to vanilla DSGD with a heterogeneity condition (A5) for non-convex costs that is admittedly slightly stronger than the average-heterogeneity condition in [11]; extension to gradient tracking / PL costs / heavy-tailed noise is deferred to future work, so the contribution does not cover the more practically relevant algorithmic variants.

The theoretical constants are large and the step-size conditions quite intricate (e.g., the constraint on C in Theorem 1, the t0 requirements in Theorem 2), which may limit practical guidance; the theory is validated only on synthetic strongly convex quadratic problems, not on more realistic (e.g., non-convex ML) tasks.

The experiments measure the empirical tail probability via Monte Carlo sampling of runs, which is a proxy for the true tail probability and involves a fairly specific simulation design; no comparison against baselines such as [57] is provided empirically.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated gap: existing HP convergence results for decentralized SGD require restrictive assumptions (uniformly bounded gradients, asymptotically vanishing noise), and the paper closes this gap by showing HP convergence under essentially the same conditions as MSE convergence.

The claim of the first HP linear speed-up in the number of users for DSGD is significant and well-supported by the analysis; Appendix J convincingly explains why prior approaches (e.g., [58] via [31, 32]) structurally cannot achieve this, which strengthens the argument for the necessity of the new technical machinery.

Several technical results appear genuinely novel and of independent interest: the HP variance-reduction result (Lemma 2), the MGF bound on the consensus gap for strongly convex costs (Lemma 4), and the 'almost decreasing process' MGF bound (Lemma 5), which the authors show is sharper than centralized-state-of-the-art bounds.

The proofs are complete and detailed (Appendices C-G); spot-checks of the proofs of Lemma 2, Lemma 5, and Theorem 1 did not reveal gaps, and the 'offset trick' argument for removing bounded gradients is clearly presented.

The paper compares favorably and precisely with the closest work [58], with detailed discussions (Appendices F, J, I) of why the improvements are possible, and derives transient times that match or strictly improve MSE-based results.
Experiments (Appendix H) empirically confirm the two main qualitative predictions: exponentially decaying tails and linear speed-up, on strongly convex costs with unbounded gradients.

Honest and thorough treatment of limitations: the log(d) dimension dependence is explicitly discussed (Section 4, Appendix L) with an explanation of where it arises and why it may be inherent, and assumption (A5) being slightly stronger than average heterogeneity is acknowledged.
weaknesses: The results are restricted to light-tailed (sub-Gaussian) noise; heavy-tailed noise, which is arguably more relevant to practice per the paper's own motivation, is deferred to future work.

The step-size conditions in Theorem 1 involve unknown problem constants (e.g., σ, λ, B), making the theoretically optimal step-sizes not directly implementable; this is standard in the literature but limits practical guidance.

The linear speed-up for non-convex costs requires a known time horizon (fixed step-size); the unknown-horizon regime loses speed-up, which is acknowledged but slightly weakens the practical scope of the headline claim.
Experiments are limited to synthetic quadratic objectives with Gaussian noise; no validation on non-convex or realistic machine learning problems, and no comparison against baselines like [58].

For strongly convex costs the analysis requires identical initialization across users (removal at cost of an extra decaying term is mentioned but not shown), and (A6) imposes twice continuous differentiability.

There are minor presentation issues, e.g., typos ('minumum', 'provide further discuss on'), and Theorem 2's statement in the main text hides some higher-order terms that are significant constants in the appendix version; also the manuscript cites several arXiv preprints by the same author group, and independent verification of Lemma 5's sharpness claims is difficult.

The non-convex case uses the max-type heterogeneity condition (A5), which is admitted to be slightly stronger than the average heterogeneity condition of [11]; the relaxation is claimed feasible but not carried out.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing HP convergence results for decentralized SGD require uniformly bounded gradients or asymptotically vanishing noise, unlike the MSE literature. The claim that DSGD converges in HP under essentially the same cost assumptions as MSE convergence is a meaningful contribution.

The linear speed-up result in the HP sense is presented as a first, and the supporting technical machinery (Lemma 2 on HP variance reduction, Lemma 4 on the MGF of the consensus gap, Lemma 5 on 'almost decreasing' processes) is plausibly novel and of independent interest, particularly Lemma 5 which improves on MGF control in [31, 32, 40].

The proofs provided in the appendix are detailed, largely self-contained, and the derivation steps I traced (e.g., Lemma 2 via norm-sub-Gaussianity and the layer-cake argument, Lemma 5 via log-MGF recursion and Darboux sums) appear correct.

The comparison with the closest work [58] is substantive rather than superficial: it identifies precisely which assumptions (path-wise bounded gradients, vanishing noise) were needed before and explains why the new lemmas remove them.

Limitations are discussed honestly and in depth, including the log(d) dependence in Appendix L, the loss of linear speed-up under unknown time horizons (Appendix F), and the requirement of shared initialization for Theorem 2.
weaknesses: The main results carry caveats that reduce their practical reach. For non-convex costs, linear speed-up is achieved only under a fixed step-size requiring a known time horizon and knowledge of problem constants (σ, L, λ); the unknown-horizon variant in Appendix F loses linear speed-up. This limits applicability relative to how the abstract presents the result.

The log(d) factor in the bounds is a genuine regression relative to both MSE results [11] and the HP bounds of [58]; it appears in the leading term of the strongly convex bound (σ²κ(1+log(2d)) in Theorem 2). While the authors argue it cannot be trivially removed, it weakens the claimed 'closing of the gap' with MSE guarantees.

Theorem 2 requires identical initialization across all users (x_i^1 = x_j^1); while the authors note the relaxation costs a geometrically decaying term, this is a non-trivial restriction not needed in the MSE literature.

The step-size and burn-in conditions involve large constants (e.g., t0 ≥ max{1960σ²κ/µ, 5184σ²λ²κ²/(µ(1−λ)), ...} in Theorem 2, and C ≤ min of five problem-dependent quantities in Theorem 1). These constants depend on unknown quantities in practice, making the theorems primarily of theoretical interest, and the extremely slowly decaying higher-order terms (e.g., 1/(T+t0)^8, t0^6 terms) make the transient-time claims sensitive to regime assumptions.

Heterogeneity assumption (A5) uses a max over users, which the authors concede is slightly stronger than the average heterogeneity used in [11]; this is acknowledged but leaves the HP/MSE assumption mismatch not fully closed.

The experiments (Appendix H) are confined to synthetic strongly convex quadratics with Gaussian noise. They validate tail decay and speed-up but do not test any of the assumptions central to the contribution (e.g., unbounded gradients in a more realistic setting), and no comparison against baseline algorithms or [58] is provided.

For the strongly convex case, the analysis covers only time-varying step-sizes with heavy burn-in terms containing Δf and ∥x^1 − x*∥²; the fixed step-size variant is only sketched and omitted, leaving the tightness discussion somewhat incomplete.

strengths: The paper closes a well-motivated gap in the decentralized optimization literature: it shows DSGD converges in high probability under essentially the same cost conditions (smoothness, lower-bounded cost, light-tailed noise) as required for MSE convergence, removing the uniformly bounded gradient and asymptotically vanishing noise assumptions of [58].

The claim of being the first work to establish linear speed-up in the number of users in the HP sense for DSGD is well supported: Lemma 2 (variance reduction of the average noise in HP), Lemma 4 (MGF of the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity), and Lemma 5 ('almost decreasing' processes) form a coherent technical toolkit, and Appendix J convincingly explains why prior MGF techniques ([31, 32, 40]) cannot yield linear speed-up.

The rates are order-optimal (O(1/sqrt(nT)) non-convex, O(1/(nT)) strongly convex) and the transient-time analysis (Appendix I) shows matching or strictly sharper transient times than MSE results, which is a strong tightness signal.

Proofs are unusually complete and self-contained: all main lemmas (2, 3, 5, 8, 11, 4) are proven in full with detailed step-size condition verification, and the step-size feasibility in Theorems 1-2 is explicitly checked.

Limitations are handled honestly and transparently: the log(d) dependence and its origin are dissected in Appendix L (including the regime where it can be removed), the loss of linear speed-up with unknown time horizon / time-varying step-size is explicitly acknowledged in Appendix F, and the marginally stronger max-heterogeneity assumption (A5) versus average heterogeneity is openly discussed.

Numerical experiments (Appendix H) validate both the exponential tail decay and the linear speed-up in a setting with unbounded gradients, directly illustrating the removal of bounded-gradient assumptions.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is limited to strongly convex quadratic objectives with Gaussian noise; the non-convex theory (Theorem 1) is not tested, and there are no experiments on standard ML losses (logistic regression, neural nets), so the practical relevance of the HP guarantees beyond synthetic instances remains unverified.

The linear speed-up results for non-convex costs require a fixed step-size with known time horizon; in the unknown-horizon regime the speed-up is lost (Appendix F), which weakens the headline claim somewhat, although this matches known MSE behavior.

Assumption (A5) is slightly stronger than the average heterogeneity condition used in comparable MSE work [11]; the authors admit a relaxation is likely possible but leave it to future work, so the 'same conditions as MSE' claim is not fully literally true for non-convex costs.
The bounds carry a log(d) factor absent from both MSE results and [58]; while mild and honestly discussed, this is an intrinsic cost of the current approach and not clearly removable.

Some presentation inconsistencies: Lemma 2 is stated under (A4) in the main text but under (A3) in the appendix restatement (and the proof internally cites (A3) where (A4) is meant); notation sigma vs. sigma-bar is occasionally conflated in the discussion of Theorem 1.

The improvement over the closest work [58], while substantial, is of an incremental character in scope (vanilla DSGD, static networks, light-tailed noise); extensions to PL costs, gradient tracking, and heavy-tailed noise are deferred to future work, leaving the coverage narrower than the general decentralized toolkit.
